title: Let the Redeemed Say So
sum: Psalm 107 opens Book Five of the Psalter with the temple's old call, "Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good." Those the LORD has redeemed and gathered from the lands are to say so. Four short stories follow, each with the same shape: travelers lost in the desert, prisoners in the dark, fools sick to the point of death, and sailors caught in a storm. Each group is in a tight place, cries to the LORD, is rescued, and is called to thank him "for his loyal love, and for the wonders he does for human beings".

The last part is a hymn about how God turns things around: rivers to desert and desert to springs, nobles sent wandering and the needy set high. It ends like a wisdom book: "Who is wise? Let him take note of these things." In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 106, and in the Greek it is headed "Alleluia", the word that ends Psalm 106 in the Hebrew.

views.H: The psalm has no title. Its first readers would have heard in it the return from Babylon: "gathered from the lands" (107:3), prisoners freed from bronze gates (107:16), and a God who makes the wilderness a pond of water (107:35), all language of Isaiah's prophecies of return.
views.C: Most scholars date the psalm after the exile and see two parts joined: a thanksgiving liturgy with four scenes and refrains (107:1–32) and a wisdom hymn (107:33–43) that borrows lines from Job. The four groups may once have been real worshipers bringing thank offerings at a festival. Its place at the start of Book Five answers the plea that ends Psalm 106.
views.L: The refrain has made Psalm 107 a psalm for anyone rescued from danger. The storm scene (107:23–32) is the sailors' psalm, read at services for those at sea. Jewish practice makes it the basis of the blessing of thanks (birkat hagomel) said after a sea voyage, a desert journey, release from prison or recovery from illness.
views.J: The Talmud draws the four scenes into Jewish law: those who cross the sea, cross the desert, recover from sickness or are freed from prison must give thanks (Bavli Berakhot 54b), and today they say the gomel blessing in the synagogue. The Midrash reads the gathered exiles as Israel brought home from all four directions.
views.X: The church fathers read the four rescues as pictures of the soul's salvation: from wandering, from the prison of sin, from sickness of soul, and from the storm of this world. The Gospels' story of Jesus stilling the storm (Mark 4:35–41) recalls 107:29, and the sending of God's word to heal (107:20) was read of Christ, the Word.

deep.b:
Each scene follows the same steps, marked by two refrains:

SceneTroubleCry and rescueThanks
Lost travelers107:4–5107:6–7107:8–9
Prisoners107:10–12107:13–14107:15–16
Fools, sick107:17–18107:19–20107:21–22
Sailors107:23–27107:28–30107:31–32

The second and third trouble come from rebellion and folly (107:11, 17); the first and fourth simply happen. The rescue is the same either way. The closing hymn (107:33–43) drops the refrains and widens the view from four rescues to the way God governs the whole land.

For this part of the Psalms the writer checked these witnesses directly: the Leningrad Codex (the Masoretic Text, with its marginal readings); the Old Greek in the Sixtine edition, which prints Codex Vaticanus, as edited by Tischendorf (1877); and the Qumran psalm scrolls in the transcription of Abegg, Bowley and Cook (4QPs-b, 4QPs-e, 4QPs-f, 4QPs-o, 4Q98f, 11QPs-a, 11QPs-b and 11QPs-d all preserve parts of Psalms 107–118). Rahlfs' Greek is cited where it differs from Vaticanus. The medieval Hebrew manuscripts, Jerome's two Latin Psalters, the Targum and the Syriac are reported from the standard editions and commentaries (Allen; Hossfeld and Zenger; Stec's Targum).

settings.what: A thanksgiving liturgy with four scenes, ending in a wisdom hymn
settings.by: A temple singer or leader, speaking for the community
settings.to: The congregation, called to give thanks, and the wise who will reflect
settings.when: No title. Scholars: after the exile, when Jews came back from many lands; some think the four scenes were sung over thank offerings at a festival
settings.why: To call every rescued person to give thanks in public, and to teach that God's loyal love can be seen in the turns of history. As the first psalm of Book Five it answers Psalm 106's plea to be gathered from the nations.
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, praying and singing the collected Psalter in the rebuilt temple, at the festivals and in their homes. Many of them had come back from far places, and some had known prison, sickness or the sea; each could find his own story among the four.
views: Mowinckel and others: four groups of pilgrims at a feast, each with a thank offering.
The four scenes as pictures of the exile and homecoming.

title: My Heart Is Firm
sum: Psalm 108 is made of two earlier psalms. Verses 1–5 repeat 57:7–11, a song of praise at dawn: "My heart is firm, God. / I will sing; I will play music." Verses 6–13 repeat 60:5–12: a prayer for rescue, God's promise to divide and claim the land and its neighbors, and a closing trust that "With God we will do mighty things."

The Plain uses the site's wording of Psalms 57 and 60 wherever the Hebrew is the same; the notes show the small differences. The laments that opened both earlier psalms are gone, so Psalm 108 moves straight from praise to promise to plea. In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 107.

views.H: The title gives the psalm to David, as the titles of 57 and 60 do. Those titles set the parts in David's life, hiding from Saul in the cave and fighting Edom and Aram; Psalm 108 keeps the words but not the stories, and has no setting of its own.
views.C: Scholars see a deliberate new psalm from the time after the exile, made by joining two older pieces. With Edom then hostile and holding land in southern Judah, God's promise over Moab, Edom and Philistia became a prayer for the restored community. The joining shows how the Psalter's editors reused older songs.
views.L: The opening, "My heart is firm ... I will wake the dawn", has long been a morning prayer. In the Orthodox and Catholic hours it is sung under its Greek number, 107. Christians and Jews pray it as a whole, praise first and need second, without the old laments.
views.J: Rashi and the Midrash read the promise over Moab, Edom and Philistia as God's word to David, and also as a promise to Israel in exile that the nations who oppressed it will one day submit. Edom in later Jewish reading stood for Rome.
views.X: Augustine and later Christian commentators read the dawn praise as Christ's resurrection morning and the claim on the nations as the gospel going out to them. The phrase "rescue by human beings is empty" (108:12) is a common Christian motto of trust.

settings.what: A new psalm made from parts of two older ones
settings.by: The title names David; the singer speaks for the people ("us", 108:11)
settings.to: God, with the oracle quoted from God himself
settings.when: The title gives no event. Scholars: a compiler after the exile joined 57:7–11 and 60:5–12, perhaps when Edom was pressing on Judah's south
settings.why: To turn two older prayers into a single song of trust: praise at dawn, God's claim on the whole land, and the plea that he march out with Israel's armies again.
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, praying and singing the collected Psalter in the rebuilt temple, at the festivals and in their homes. Living in a small province, they could pray that the land God had promised, and the neighbors who had wronged them, were still under his rule.

title: They Curse, but You Bless
sum: A man falsely accused prays to "God, the one I praise". His enemies have answered his love with lies and hatred, and his only answer is prayer. Then comes the longest string of curses in the Psalms (109:6–19): let a wicked man judge him and an accuser stand at his right hand, let his days be few and another take over his charge, let his children beg and his name be erased. He loved cursing, so let it be his clothing.

The prayer turns with "But you, LORD, my Lord": the singer is poor and needy, thin from fasting, mocked with tossing heads. "They curse, and you bless." It ends with praise for the God who stands at the needy one's right hand. Peter applies 109:8 to Judas in Acts 1:20. In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 108.
readings: The traditional reading: the speaker himself calls down the curses on his chief enemy, as the victim of lies who brings his case to the judge of all. Acts 1:20 reads it this way when it applies 109:8 to Judas.
Read as the enemies' curse, quoted

Many recent scholars take 109:6–19 as the curse the accusers spoke against the singer, which he repeats to God before asking for help (109:20–21). The change from "they" to "he" supports this; nothing in the Hebrew marks a quotation.

The church read the psalm in Christ's voice, against Judas and against evil: the betrayer whose office another took (Acts 1:20), the head-tossing mockers (Matthew 27:39), and Christ's own answer of prayer and blessing (Luke 23:34).

views.H: The title says "Of David" and gives no event. Readers have thought of the men who betrayed David: Doeg, who informed on him (1 Samuel 22:9–10), Ahithophel, his counselor who joined Absalom (2 Samuel 15:31), or Shimei, who cursed him (2 Samuel 16:5–8).
views.C: Form critics call Psalm 109 an individual lament of the falsely accused, probably prayed at the sanctuary as part of a legal process (109:7, 31). They disagree about 109:6–19; Erich Zenger and others take them as the enemies' words. Ancient Near Eastern treaties and legal texts use curses of the same kind.
views.L: The psalm is one of the three left out of the Catholic Liturgy of the Hours (with 58 and 83). It is still read in full in the Orthodox Psalter, in the monthly Anglican cycle and by churches that sing only psalms. Many prayer books bracket 109:6–19.
views.J: Jewish interpreters read the psalm as David's prayer against Doeg and Ahithophel, or as Israel's prayer against its persecutors. It is not part of the regular synagogue liturgy. The Midrash stresses that David prayed rather than took revenge (109:4).
views.X: Augustine read the psalm as a prophecy of Judas and of those who reject Christ, not as personal revenge. Christian writers have also stressed that the psalm hands vengeance over to God (Romans 12:19) and that the singer's own answer is "I am all prayer" and "you bless". C. S. Lewis called the cursing psalms terrible but honest, and Bonhoeffer said Christians pray them through Christ.

deep.b:
Readers have taken several approaches, which can be combined:

  • Justice, not revenge. The curses are a plea to the judge, in the language of the law court, against a man who "chased down the poor and the needy" (109:16). Nothing in the psalm says the singer will act himself.
  • Measure for measure. He loved cursing, so let it come to him (109:17–19); he showed no loyal love, so let none be shown him (109:12, 16).
  • Words of the enemy. If 109:6–19 quotes the accusers, the singer himself curses no one (see the note on 109:6).
  • Prophecy. Acts 1:20 and Augustine read the curses as what would come on the betrayer of Christ.
  • Handed over to God. The psalm moves from curse to "But you, LORD" (109:21) and "They curse, and you bless" (109:28). Praying it can mean giving anger to God instead of acting on it.

For other curse psalms see the topic page and Psalms 35, 69 and 137.

Parts of Psalm 109 survive in three scrolls: 4QPs-e (109:1, 8, 13), 4QPs-f (109:4–7, 24–28) and 11QPs-a (109:21–31), with a few words in 11QPs-b (109:3–4). Their text is close to the Masoretic Text. 4QPs-f spells the word for "accuse" with a samekh, yistemuni (109:4), and 11QPs-a puts "LORD" before "you" in 109:27. In 11QPs-a the psalm stands in a different place: after Psalms 101, 102 and 103 and just before Psalm 118 and then 104. That arrangement is one of the main signs that the order of the last part of the Psalter was not yet fixed in every community.

settings.what: A lament of a falsely accused man, with curses and a vow of praise
settings.by: A poor and needy man under false accusation; the title names David
settings.to: God, as judge; the curses speak of the chief enemy
settings.when: The title: David, with no event named. Scholars: a prayer at the sanctuary during a legal case, when the accused asked God to judge
settings.why: To bring an unbearable injustice to God instead of taking revenge, to ask the judge to turn the curse back on the one who loved cursing, and to promise praise when God stands at the needy one's right hand.
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, praying and singing the collected Psalter in the rebuilt temple, at the festivals and in their homes. Many of them were poor and in debt (Nehemiah 5:1–5), and they knew what it was to be cursed and accused by stronger men.
views: The traditional reading, and that of Acts 1:20.
Zenger, Kraus and others: 109:6–19 report what the accusers said.

traditions.q: Should a curse psalm such as Psalm 109 be prayed in public worship?
views: The Liturgy of the Hours leaves out Psalms 58, 83 and 109 entirely, and some verses of others, because of the "psychological difficulty" they cause, though they remain Scripture (General Instruction of the Liturgy of the Hours 131).

Psalm 109 (Greek 108) is read with the rest of the Psalter in the weekly cycle of kathismata. Orthodox commentators, following the Fathers, read it of Judas and of spiritual enemies rather than of people.

Churches that sing only psalms sing it in full. Calvin held that David spoke by the Spirit as a type of Christ, not from private anger, and warned that no one may use the psalm to curse a personal enemy.
The Book of Common Prayer (1662) appoints the whole Psalter, Psalm 109 included, in its monthly cycle; many later psalters mark the curse verses so that they may be left out.
Bonhoeffer taught that Christians may pray the curse psalms because Christ, the innocent sufferer, prayed them and took God's judgment on himself, praying for his enemies.

title: Sit at My Right Hand
sum: A prophet brings the LORD's word to the king: "Sit at my right hand, until I set your enemies down as a stool for your feet." The LORD will send the king's scepter out from Zion; his people offer themselves freely on the day of battle. Then God swears an oath: "You are a priest forever, after the pattern of Melchizedek." The Lord at the king's right hand shatters kings and judges the nations, and the king drinks from a stream on the way and lifts his head.

It is the psalm the New Testament quotes most. Jesus asks how the Messiah can be David's son if David calls him "my lord"; the apostles proclaim the risen Jesus seated at God's right hand; Hebrews builds its teaching on Christ's priesthood on 110:4. Verse 3 is one of the hardest in the Bible, and the Hebrew and Greek read it very differently. In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 109.
readings: Most scholars: a prophet at the crowning of a king in Jerusalem announces God's promises to him, rule over his enemies and an old priest-kingship like Melchizedek's. The king of David's line is seated at God's right as God's deputy, as in Psalm 2.

The Talmud and Rashi read "my lord" as Abraham, who defeated the kings and met Melchizedek (Genesis 14); others read David, spoken of by a court singer, and some midrashim the Messiah. Justin Martyr reports that Jewish teachers of his day applied the psalm to King Hezekiah (Dialogue with Trypho 33; 83).

Jesus' question (Mark 12:35–37) and the apostles' preaching (Acts 2:34–36) make the "lord" the Messiah, greater than David, raised and seated at God's right hand. Hebrews 5–7 reads 110:4 as Christ's eternal priesthood, and the creeds confess that he "sits at the right hand of the Father".

views.H: The title gives the psalm to David, and Jesus' argument rests on it: David, speaking by the Spirit, calls someone else "my lord" (Mark 12:36). If David wrote it, he speaks of a king after him; read with his newly won Jerusalem, the city of Melchizedek, the priest-king of the psalm fits David's own capture of the city (2 Samuel 5:6–9).
views.C: Most critical scholars date the psalm to the time of the kings, perhaps early, and read it as a royal coronation oracle; the title means "for David" or "belonging to the David collection". The Melchizedek line may claim the old Jebusite priest-kingship of Jerusalem for the new dynasty. A few have dated it to the Maccabean priest-kings, whose leaders took both titles; most reject that date.
views.L: The church sings Psalm 110 at Vespers every Sunday in the Roman rite, with 110:4 as an antiphon, and on feasts of the priesthood. Its first line is in the creeds. The Latin Dixit Dominus is one of the most often set texts in church music, by Monteverdi, Vivaldi and Handel among others.
views.J: The Talmud reads 110:4 as God's oath to Abraham, who received the priesthood once held by Melchizedek (Bavli Nedarim 32b), and Rashi reads the whole psalm of Abraham's victory over the kings (Genesis 14). Medieval Jewish writers in debates with Christians, such as Nachmanides at Barcelona in 1263, answered the Christian reading of "my lord" by pointing to the human title adoni.
views.X: For the New Testament, Psalm 110 shows who Jesus is: David's son and David's Lord, seated at God's right hand until every enemy is under his feet, and priest forever after Melchizedek's pattern. The church fathers used the Greek of 110:3, "before the morning star I fathered you", for his eternal birth from the Father.

David Hay counted some thirty-three quotations and allusions in the New Testament, more than for any other Old Testament text. In the earliest Christian preaching the verse explained Easter: the crucified one had been raised, not only from death but to God's throne.

Melchizedek appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible: in Genesis 14:18–20, where the king of Salem brings out bread and wine, blesses Abram and receives a tenth, and in 110:4. His name means "my king is righteousness" or "king of righteousness", and Salem is Jerusalem (76:2). Later readers filled the gaps in different ways. The Genesis Apocryphon from Qumran retells the meeting with Abram; 11QMelchizedek makes him a heavenly judge who brings release at the end of days; Philo makes him a picture of reason; the Talmud identifies him with Shem; Hebrews takes his missing genealogy as a picture of a priest who lives forever. The Roman Canon of the Mass names his offering beside Abel's and Abraham's, and Christian art and the Catechism (1333) see his bread and wine as a figure of the Eucharist. See the topic page.

echoes: 2:6–9; 89:27; Genesis 14:18–20; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Daniel 7:13; Mark 12:35–37; Mark 14:62; Acts 2:34–36; 1 Corinthians 15:25; Hebrews 1:13; Hebrews 5:6; Hebrews 7:1–28

settings.what: A royal oracle: God's words to the king, with an oath
settings.by: A prophet or court singer, passing on "the LORD's declaration"; the title names David
settings.when: The title: David. Scholars: the coronation of a king of David's line in Jerusalem, during the monarchy
settings.why: To announce God's promises to the new king: a seat at God's right hand, victory, a willing people, and an eternal priesthood like Melchizedek's. It tied the dynasty to God's rule from Zion.
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, praying and singing the collected Psalter in the rebuilt temple, at the festivals and in their homes. With no king on the throne, they read the promises as still to come, for the king God would send; that is how the psalm became a text of messianic hope.
views: David speaks of a greater lord
The title as Jesus read it (Mark 12:36).
A court prophet speaks to the king
Most critical scholars: "my lord" is the reigning king.

traditions.q: What does "a priest forever, after the pattern of Melchizedek" (110:4) mean for Christian ministers?
views: Christ is the one high priest after Melchizedek's order; ordained priests share in his priesthood and offer the one sacrifice of the Mass (Catechism 1544–1545). The Roman Canon names Melchizedek's offering, and the Catechism sees his bread and wine as a figure of the Eucharist (Catechism 1333; compare 1544).
Christ is the eternal high priest; the bishop and priest stand in his place at the Eucharist and are true priests by his gift, and Melchizedek's offering is a type of the Eucharist.

Christ's sacrifice was offered once for all; the Mass is not a sacrifice that earns forgiveness, and ministers are servants of Word and Sacrament rather than sacrificing priests (Apology of the Augsburg Confession 24).

Christ's priesthood is unique and is not passed on to anyone; the Lord's Supper is not a sacrifice but a memorial of his one offering (Westminster Confession 29.2). All believers share a priesthood of praise.

The "Melchizedek Priesthood" is a real, higher priesthood restored in the latter days and held by worthy men in the church today, named after Melchizedek out of reverence for the name of God (Doctrine and Covenants 107:1–4).

title: Great Are the LORD's Works
sum: After a Hallelujah, Psalm 111 praises God's works in 22 short lines, each beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from alef to tav. The LORD's works are great and worth study; he has set up a memorial of his wonders; he is gracious and compassionate, feeds those who fear him, keeps his covenant, gave his people the land, and sent them redemption. It ends with a motto of the wisdom books: "Wisdom starts with the fear of the LORD."

Psalm 112 has exactly the same plan and many of the same words, now applied to the person who fears God. The letters of the alphabet are listed below. In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 110.

views.H: The psalm has no title beyond "Praise the LORD!". The works it praises are those of Israel's history: the wonders of the exodus, food in the wilderness, the covenant, and the gift of "the nations as their inheritance" (111:6), the land of Canaan.
views.C: Scholars class it as a hymn in wisdom style, written after the exile by a teacher who used the alphabet form. Its many phrases from Exodus and Deuteronomy show a writer steeped in the Torah. Psalms 111 and 112 were composed as a pair, and the Hallelujah links them with 113 and the Hallel.
views.L: Christians have long sung 111:4–5 at the Eucharist and on Corpus Christi: a memorial of wonders, food for those who fear him. Its Latin Confitebor tibi Domine is a Sunday Vespers psalm, set by Monteverdi, Vivaldi and Mozart. Its second verse is carved over the doors of the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge.
views.J: Its last verse, "Wisdom starts with the fear of the LORD", opens the morning prayers in some Jewish rites. Jewish commentators read "a memorial of his wonders" as the Sabbath and the festivals, by which Israel remembers what God did.
views.X: Christian writers read "he sent his people redemption" (111:9) with Zechariah's song (Luke 1:68) as the coming of Christ, and the memorial and food (111:4–5) as the Lord's Supper. The fathers also read the "food" of 111:5 as the bread from heaven (John 6:31–35).

settings.what: An alphabet hymn of praise in wisdom style
settings.by: A teacher and worshiper ("I will give the LORD thanks")
settings.to: The congregation and the circle of the upright, who hear God praised
settings.when: No title but "Praise the LORD!". Scholars: after the exile, among teachers of the Torah
settings.why: To praise God's works in Israel's history in an order easy to learn by heart, and to lead the hearer to the fear of the LORD, where wisdom starts.
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, praying and singing the collected Psalter in the rebuilt temple, at the festivals and in their homes. Its alphabet form suited teaching in homes and schools, and its memorial of wonders pointed to the festivals they kept.

title: Happy Is the One Who Fears the LORD
sum: The twin of Psalm 111, with the same alphabet plan, from alef to tav. "Happy is the person who fears the LORD." His children will be strong, his house well supplied, his righteousness lasting. A light rises for him in the dark; he is gracious and lends, and he is not afraid of bad news, because his heart trusts in the LORD. He has given freely to the poor. The wicked man sees it, grinds his teeth and melts away.

Many of its words are borrowed from Psalm 111, so that the God-fearing person comes to look like God: righteous for all time, gracious and compassionate. Paul quotes 112:9 in 2 Corinthians 9:9. The letters are listed below. In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 111.

views.H: Like Psalm 111 it has no author, only "Praise the LORD!". It describes a well-off householder in an Israelite town: a family, a house, money to lend, a name in the community.
views.C: Scholars read it as a wisdom poem written as the pair to Psalm 111, after the exile. It shares the outlook of Psalm 1 and Proverbs: the righteous flourish, the wicked fade. The doubled phrase "his righteousness stands for all time" (111:3; 112:3, 9) ties the two psalms together.
views.L: The Latin Beatus vir is a Sunday Vespers psalm, often set to music (Monteverdi, Vivaldi). Churches read 112:9 with 2 Corinthians 9 at offerings and in teaching on generosity. 112:7, "He does not fear bad news", is a favorite verse of comfort.
views.J: Jewish tradition reads the psalm as a portrait of the generous man, and 112:9 became a text for tsedaqah, charity. The Talmud reads "Happy is the man" (ish, a man or person) as "happy is the one who repents while he is still a man", in his strength (Bavli Avodah Zarah 19a).
views.X: Paul uses 112:9 to encourage giving to the poor in Jerusalem (2 Corinthians 9:9). The church fathers read the "person who fears the LORD" first of Christ, the truly righteous one, and then of the saints who imitate him. Some modern preachers have read the promise of wealth as a guarantee, a reading most churches reject.

Words borrowed from Psalm 111 include "his righteousness stands for all time" (111:3; 112:3, 9), "gracious and compassionate" (111:4; 112:4), and "propped firm" (111:8; 112:8).

settings.what: An alphabet poem in wisdom style, the pair of Psalm 111
settings.to: The listener, who is shown what the God-fearing life looks like
settings.when: No title but "Praise the LORD!". Scholars: after the exile, written with Psalm 111
settings.why: To portray the person who fears God as reflecting God's own goodness, generous and unafraid, and to encourage readers to live that way.
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, praying and singing the collected Psalter in the rebuilt temple, at the festivals and in their homes. In a small, often poor community, its picture of the generous lender and giver set out what a good neighbor should be.

title: Who Is Like the LORD Our God?
sum: Psalm 113 opens the Hallel, the six psalms (113–118) sung at Passover and the great festivals. Servants of the LORD are called to praise his name from now on and from east to west. He is high over the nations and the heavens, and yet he bends down low to look, lifting the poor out of the dust and the needy from the garbage heap to sit with nobles. The childless woman becomes a glad mother of children.

Verses 7–8 are almost word for word from Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:8), and Mary's song in Luke 1 takes up the same themes. At the Passover meal, families sing this psalm before the meal. In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 112.

views.H: The psalm has no title. Its first and last word is "Praise the LORD!" Its picture of a barren woman made a mother recalls Hannah, whose song it echoes, and Sarah and Rachel before her.
views.C: Scholars class it as a hymn, perhaps from after the exile, built in three parts: a call to praise (113:1–3), God's height and stooping (113:4–6), and the lowly lifted (113:7–9). Its borrowing from 1 Samuel 2 suggests a stock of hymn language shared by both.
views.L: In Jewish worship Psalm 113 begins the Hallel on festivals and at the Passover Seder, where it is sung before the meal. In Christian worship it is a Vespers psalm (Laudate pueri), and many churches read it with Mary's song (Luke 1:46–55).
views.J: The Mishnah records the debate on how much of the Hallel to sing before the Passover meal: the house of Shammai said up to "a glad mother of children" (113:9), the house of Hillel up to "flint into a fountain" (114:8) (Mishnah Pesachim 10:6). The Midrash reads the barren woman as Zion, empty in exile and filled with her children again.
views.X: Christians hear in the God who "bends down low to look" the coming of the Son to earth (Philippians 2:6–8), and in the lifting of the lowly the theme of Mary's song. The fathers read the barren woman as the church of the nations, made mother of many (Galatians 4:27).

deep.b: The Mishnah describes the Hallel in two places. In the temple, the Levites sang it while each group of worshipers slaughtered their Passover lambs, repeating it if needed (Mishnah Pesachim 5:7). At the evening meal the family sang the first part after the second cup, before eating, and finished it over the fourth cup (Mishnah Pesachim 10:6–7). The two schools differed on where to break: after Psalm 113 (Shammai) or after 114 (Hillel). The Passover Haggadah today follows Hillel: 113–114 before the meal, 115–118 after it. The Gospels' "they sang the hymn" (Mark 14:26; Matthew 26:30) is commonly taken as the second half.

echoes: 1 Samuel 2:1–10; Exodus 15:11; Isaiah 57:15; Isaiah 54:1; Luke 1:46–55; Philippians 2:6–8; Galatians 4:27

settings.what: A hymn of praise opening the Hallel
settings.to: "Servants of the LORD", the worshipers or the temple's Levites
settings.when: No title. Scholars: temple worship, probably after the exile; later sung at Passover and the pilgrim festivals
settings.why: To praise the God who is above everything and yet stoops to raise the poor and give the childless a family.
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, praying and singing the collected Psalter in the rebuilt temple, at the festivals and in their homes. For a people brought low by the exile, the God who lifts the poor from the dust was a reason for hope and a song for every festival.

title: When Israel Went Out from Egypt
sum: A short, vivid poem of the exodus. When Israel left Egypt, Judah became God's holy place and Israel his domain. The sea saw and ran; the Jordan turned backward; the mountains leapt like rams. The poet asks them what happened, and answers: let the whole earth writhe before the Lord, the God of Jacob, who turns rock into a pond of water and flint into a fountain.

The poem does not name God until 114:7. It joins the Red Sea crossing, Sinai and the Jordan crossing into one picture. It is the second psalm of the Hallel, the one that gave it the name "Egyptian Hallel". The Greek and Latin join Psalms 114 and 115 into one psalm, Psalm 113.

views.H: The psalm has no title and tells Israel's oldest story: the exodus from Egypt, the sea, Sinai's trembling, the Jordan, and the water from the rock.
views.C: Scholars admire it as one of the most finished poems in the Psalter, with its tight parallel lines and its delayed naming of God. Some date it early, from northern Israel, because it speaks of Judah and Israel together; most place it with the Hallel after the exile. The fleeing sea and river echo Canaanite myths of Sea and River as one enemy.
views.L: It is sung at the Passover Seder before the meal and in the synagogue Hallel. In the medieval church In exitu Israel was sung at funerals as the body was carried to the grave, and Dante's souls sing it as they arrive at Purgatory.
views.J: The Midrash says the sea fled because it saw the bones of Joseph carried out of Egypt (Exodus 13:19). The Talmud reads "Judah became his holy place" as praise for the tribe of Judah, whose prince Nahshon was first into the sea (Bavli Sotah 37a).
views.X: Christians read the exodus as a picture of baptism and of passing from death to life (1 Corinthians 10:1–4), and the rock that gave water as Christ. Dante's letter uses 114:1 to explain the four senses of Scripture: history, Christ, the soul's conversion, and the passage to glory.

echoes: Exodus 14:21–22; Exodus 17:1–7; Exodus 19:18; Numbers 20:2–13; Joshua 3:13–17; Joshua 4:23; 77:16–19; Habakkuk 3:8–10; 1 Corinthians 10:1–4

settings.what: A hymn of the exodus, the second psalm of the Hallel
settings.to: The sea, the Jordan, the mountains and the earth, addressed in turn
settings.when: No title. Scholars: a festival song, perhaps for Passover; dates range from the monarchy to after the exile
settings.why: To celebrate the exodus as the moment when God made Israel his own, and to call the whole earth to tremble before the God of Jacob.
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, praying and singing the collected Psalter in the rebuilt temple, at the festivals and in their homes. At Passover they sang it as their own story; the God who once turned rock into water could bring them through their own wilderness.

title: Not to Us
sum: "Not to us, LORD, not to us, but to your own name give glory." The nations taunt, "So where is their God?" Israel's God is in the heavens and does whatever he wants; their idols are silver and gold, with mouths that cannot speak, eyes that cannot see and feet that cannot walk, and the ones who make them will end up like them. Israel, the house of Aaron and all who fear the LORD are called to trust him: "He is their help and their shield."

The LORD will bless all three groups, small and great. The heavens are his, and the earth he has given to human beings. The dead do not praise Yah, but "we, we will bless Yah from this moment on and for all time." In the Greek and Latin this psalm is joined to Psalm 114 as Psalm 113 (115 is Greek 113:9–26).

views.H: The psalm has no title. The taunt "Where is their God?" fits a time when Israel had no king and perhaps no temple, surrounded by peoples with impressive statues of their gods.
views.C: Form critics read it as a temple liturgy with several voices: a community prayer (115:1–2), a hymn mocking idols (115:3–8), calls and responses to three groups (115:9–11), a priestly blessing (115:12–15) and a closing vow (115:16–18). Most date it after the exile; its idol satire matches Isaiah 44 and Jeremiah 10.
views.L: It is sung in the Hallel after the Passover meal and on festivals. Non nobis, Domine became a Christian hymn of thanks after victory, sung in Shakespeare's Henry V and set by many composers.
views.J: The Midrash reads "not to us" as Israel's prayer in exile: if God acts, let it be for his name and not for any merit of theirs. "You who fear the LORD" (115:11) were read by the rabbis as converts to Judaism, a group distinct from Israel and the priests.
views.X: Christians have heard in "not to us" a confession that salvation is by grace, and in the idol satire a warning against every rival to God, from statues to wealth and power. The warning of 115:8, that worshipers become like what they worship, has become a common theme in Christian teaching on idolatry.

settings.what: A temple liturgy against idols, with calls to trust and a blessing
settings.by: Several voices: the community, a leader, the priests who bless
settings.to: God (115:1), the three groups of worshipers, and the congregation
settings.when: No title. Scholars: temple worship after the exile, perhaps at a festival; later the third psalm of the Hallel
settings.why: To answer the nations' taunt by praising the living God over lifeless idols, to call all of Israel to trust him, and to bless them in his name.
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, praying and singing the collected Psalter in the rebuilt temple, at the festivals and in their homes. Under Persian and Greek rule they lived among temples full of statues, and the psalm told them that their imageless God was the real one.
views: The Greek, the Latin and some Hebrew manuscripts.
The Masoretic Text and most modern scholars.

traditions.q: "The dead do not praise Yah" (115:17). Are the dead conscious between death and resurrection?
views: Each soul is judged at death and goes at once to heaven, to purgatory or to hell, and the church prays for the dead (Catechism 1021–1032). Verses like 115:17 reflect the Old Testament before the full revelation of life after death.
The departed are alive in Christ and await the resurrection; the church prays for them and asks the saints' prayers, so the silence of Sheol is broken by Christ's descent among the dead.
The souls of the righteous are made perfect at death and received into heaven, where they behold God, awaiting the redemption of their bodies; there is no purgatory (Westminster Confession 32.1).
Death is an unconscious sleep until the resurrection; the dead know nothing and do not praise God, as 115:17, 146:4 and Ecclesiastes 9:5 say (Fundamental Belief 26).
The soul is the whole living person, and the dead are conscious of nothing; they will be raised to life on a restored earth or, for a few, in heaven. Texts such as 115:17 are read literally.

title: The Cup of Rescue
sum: "I love, because the LORD hears my voice." Death's ropes had closed around the singer, and he called on the LORD's name; the LORD, gracious and righteous, guards the simple, and he saved him. Now he tells his soul to come back to rest. He kept trusting even when he said, in a panic, "Every human being lies."

What can he give back? He will raise the cup of rescue, pay his vows in front of all the people, and bring a thank offering in the courts of the LORD's house in Jerusalem, for the death of God's loyal ones weighs heavily in his eyes. Paul quotes 116:10 in 2 Corinthians 4:13. In the Greek and Latin the psalm is split in two: 116:1–9 is Psalm 114 and 116:10–19 is Psalm 115.

views.H: The psalm has no title. The singer has been near death, probably through illness, and comes to the temple with his vows and a thank offering in front of the whole people.
views.C: Form critics call it an individual song of thanksgiving, spoken at the temple over a thank offering (116:17), with a cup of wine raised in thanks (116:13). Its language borrows from older psalms (18:4–6; 86:16) and has Aramaic-looking word forms, so most date it after the exile.
views.L: At the Passover Seder it is sung after the meal; the "cup of rescue" is linked with the cups of the Seder. In the Latin Mass the priest said 116:12–13 before receiving the chalice, and many churches use 116:12–19 on Holy Thursday. "Precious in the sight of the LORD" (116:15, KJV) is read at many funerals.
views.J: The Midrash reads the singer as Israel rescued from exile, or as David. The Talmud uses "the LORD guards the simple" (116:6) in law, to allow ordinary people to rely on God's protection in some risks of daily life (for example Bavli Shabbat 129b).
views.X: Christians read the psalm as the thanks of the risen Christ, freed from death's ropes, and of every believer in him. Paul's "I believed; therefore I spoke" (2 Corinthians 4:13) and the cup of the Lord's Supper made it a eucharistic psalm. Its first verse became a model of personal love for God.

settings.what: A song of thanksgiving after rescue from death, with a vow paid at the temple
settings.by: A worshiper who has recovered from mortal danger
settings.to: God, his own soul (116:7), and the people gathered at the temple
settings.when: No title. Scholars: a thank-offering service in the temple courts in Jerusalem, after the exile
settings.why: To tell before everyone how God answered when death seemed certain, and to pay the vows made in that danger with a cup and a sacrifice of thanks.
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, praying and singing the collected Psalter in the rebuilt temple, at the festivals and in their homes. Sung after the Passover meal, it let the whole people give thanks as one person rescued from death.

title: All You Nations
sum: The shortest psalm, two verses long. All nations and peoples are called to praise the LORD, "for his loyal love is mighty over us, and the LORD's faithfulness is forever." The reason given is what God has done for Israel; the call goes to the whole world.
Paul quotes 117:1 in Romans 15:11, among texts that show the nations praising God with Israel. In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 116.

views.H: The psalm has no title. Its two words for God's character, loyal love and faithfulness (hesed and emet), are the words of God's self-description on Sinai (Exodus 34:6).
views.C: Some scholars think so short a psalm was once part of another, the end of 116 or the start of 118, and some Hebrew manuscripts join it to one of them. Most read it as a complete short hymn: a call to praise and a reason.
views.L: It is sung in the Hallel and, in Latin (Laudate Dominum omnes gentes), at Benediction in the Catholic Church and in many settings, including Mozart's and the Taizé chant. Its brevity makes it a common doxology.
views.J: Rabbinic writers asked why the nations should praise God for his love "over us", Israel, and read the psalm of the age to come, when the nations will see what God has done for Israel and recognize him.
views.X: Paul uses it for the church of Jews and Gentiles together (Romans 15:8–12). The popular claim that it is the middle chapter of the Bible depends on the count (see the note).

settings.what: A short hymn calling the nations to praise
settings.when: No title. Scholars: temple worship after the exile, as a brief call to praise within the Hallel
settings.why: To call the whole world to praise Israel's God for his loyal love and faithfulness to his people.
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, praying and singing the collected Psalter in the rebuilt temple, at the festivals and in their homes. A small people among empires, they sang that the nations too would one day praise the God of Israel.

title: His Loyal Love Is Forever
sum: The last psalm of the Hallel is a festival procession. It opens and closes with "Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good; his loyal love is forever," and Israel, the house of Aaron and all who fear the LORD answer in turn. A leader tells how all the nations closed in on him like bees and he cut them down in the LORD's name: "I will not die, for I will live and tell what Yah has done." At the gates of righteousness he asks to enter and give thanks.

Then the crowd sings of a stone the builders threw out that has become the head of the corner, "This is the day the LORD has acted", "LORD, please, save us now!" (Hosanna) and "Blessed is the one who comes in the LORD's name!" The festival offering is tied to the horns of the altar. Jesus quotes 118:22–23 of himself, the crowds greet him with 118:25–26 when he enters Jerusalem, and it was probably the end of the hymn sung after the Last Supper (Mark 14:26). In the Greek and Latin numbering this is Psalm 117.
readings: A king or leader, rescued from enemy nations, leads a procession of thanks to the temple; the priests greet him and the people celebrate. The rejected stone is the leader the nations despised.

Jewish tradition reads the speaker as Israel, surrounded by the nations, disciplined but not given up to death; Rashi makes the rejected stone Israel, and the Targum the young David. The psalm is sung on every festival in the Hallel.

Jesus applies 118:22–23 to himself (Mark 12:10–11), the crowds greet him with 118:25–26 (Mark 11:9), and Acts and 1 Peter make him the rejected cornerstone. The church sings 118:24 at Easter as the day of resurrection.

views.H: The psalm has no title. Readers have proposed settings from David's wars, Nehemiah's rebuilding of the walls despite enemies (Nehemiah 6:15–16), or the rededication of the temple under the Maccabees.
views.C: Scholars read it as a liturgy of thanksgiving with several voices: the leader, choirs, gatekeepers and priests. Many connect it with the Feast of Booths, when 118:25 was chanted around the altar and branches were carried (Mishnah Sukkah 4:5). It borrows from the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15) and closes the Hallel, which suits Passover as well.
views.L: In Jewish worship it ends the Hallel at every festival; 118:25 is chanted with the waving of the palm branch at Booths, and 118:26 greets guests and couples. In Christian worship 118:24 is the Easter antiphon Haec dies, 118:26 with "Hosanna" is sung in every Eucharist, and the psalm is used on Palm Sunday.
views.J: The Talmud divides the closing verses among David, his brothers, Jesse and Samuel, as if the psalm told David's anointing (Bavli Pesachim 119a). The Targum reads the rejected stone as the boy David.
views.X: The New Testament uses Psalm 118 more than almost any psalm except 110 and 22: the rejected stone (Mark 12:10–11; Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:7; Ephesians 2:20), Hosanna and "Blessed is the one who comes" (Mark 11:9–10; Matthew 23:39), and "What can a human being do to me?" (Hebrews 13:6). Luther called it his own psalm.

deep.h: Psalm 118 in the Gospels and letters
deep.b:
Psalm 118New Testament
118:6, the Lord my helperHebrews 13:6
118:22–23, the rejected stoneMark 12:10–11; Matthew 21:42; Luke 20:17; Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:4–8; Ephesians 2:20
118:25–26, Hosanna and the one who comesMark 11:9–10; Matthew 21:9; Luke 19:38; John 12:13
118:26, "until you say"Matthew 23:39; Luke 13:35
118:26, "the one who is coming"Matthew 11:3; Luke 7:19
Hallel after the supperMark 14:26; Matthew 26:30

The pattern follows the psalm: the one rejected by the builders and greeted by the crowds is the one God raises up. In the Gospels the stone saying comes in the last week in Jerusalem, between the entry with Hosannas and the arrest.

Read as a liturgy, the psalm moves in stages: a call to thanks and three responses (118:1–4); the leader's story of rescue (118:5–18); the request at the gate and the gatekeepers' answer (118:19–20); thanks inside (118:21); the crowd's song of the stone and the day (118:22–25); the priests' blessing from the house (118:26); the procession to the altar (118:27); the leader's vow and the closing refrain (118:28–29). At the Feast of Booths, the Mishnah says, people walked around the altar with willow branches chanting 118:25 each day, seven times on the seventh day (Mishnah Sukkah 4:5).

Psalm 118 is well preserved at Qumran, and the scrolls show it being used in more than one way.

  • 4QPs-b (4Q84) has most of the psalm. It leaves out 118:11 and reads "trust" for "take shelter" in 118:8 (see the variants).
  • 11QPs-a (11Q5) has 118:25–29 right after Psalm 109, in a sequence 101–103, 109, 118, 104. After Psalm 136 it has a second, short gathering of Psalm 118 verses: 118:1, 15, 16, 8, 9 and 29, with an extra line, "better to trust in the LORD than to trust in a thousand people". Its 118:16 ends "has done a mighty deed", and its 118:26 repeats "in the name" by mistake.
  • 11QPs-b (11Q6) has the same short gathering (118:1, 15, 16), so it was not a one-off.

The short gathering looks like a refrain or response built from Psalm 118 for use after Psalm 136, which shares its refrain "his loyal love is forever". The Plain follows the Masoretic Text in every case.

echoes: Exodus 15:2; Exodus 15:6; 115:9–11; 136:1; Isaiah 28:16; Zechariah 4:7; Mark 11:9–10; Mark 12:10–11; Mark 14:26; Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:4–8; Ephesians 2:20; Hebrews 13:6; Matthew 23:39

settings.what: The call to thanks and the leader's story of rescue
settings.by: A worship leader (118:1–4), answered by Israel, the house of Aaron and those who fear the LORD; then a rescued king or leader (118:5–18)
settings.to: The congregation, and then God and the people together
settings.when: No title. Scholars: a festival in the temple, often linked with Booths, after the exile; or a king's thanksgiving after victory
settings.why: To gather the whole people into the thanks and let the rescued one tell how the LORD saved him when the nations closed in.
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, praying and singing the collected Psalter in the rebuilt temple, at the festivals and in their homes. Each group named in 118:2–4 heard its own call to answer, and the leader's story could be heard as the story of the nation.
views: Mowinckel and others: the king leads the procession after battle.
The speaker is the nation, surrounded and saved.

settings.what: The exchange at the temple gate
settings.by: The rescued leader (118:19, 21) and the gatekeepers or priests (118:20)
settings.when: At the temple gates, as in the entry liturgies of Psalms 15 and 24
settings.why: To ask entry to the temple, to hear that only the righteous may enter, and to give thanks inside.
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, praying and singing the collected Psalter in the rebuilt temple, at the festivals and in their homes. As pilgrims at the festivals, they too stood at the gates and were let in to give thanks.

settings.what: The crowd's song, the priests' blessing and the procession to the altar
settings.by: The people (118:22–25), the priests in the temple (118:26–27) and the leader (118:28), with all at the closing refrain (118:29)
settings.to: God and one another (118:22–25); the arriving procession (118:26); God (118:28)
settings.when: Inside the temple courts, at a festival; the Mishnah describes 118:25 chanted around the altar at Booths
settings.why: To celebrate the reversal God has worked, the rejected stone made the head of the corner, to bless all who come in the LORD's name, and to lead the festival offering to the altar.
settings.readers: Israelites after the exile, praying and singing the collected Psalter in the rebuilt temple, at the festivals and in their homes. They sang it at every pilgrim festival; the rejected stone was their own story of a nation brought back from ruin.
